1[TENTH SCHEDULE
[Articles 102(2) and 191(2)]
Provisions as to disqualification on ground of defection
1. Interpretation.—In this Schedule, unless the context otherwise requires,—
(a) "House" means either House of Parliament or the Legislative
Assembly or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature of a State;
(b) "legislature party", in relation to a member of a House
belonging to any political party in accordance with the provisions of
paragraph 2 or 2*** paragraph 4, means the group consisting of all the
members of that House for the time being belonging to that political party
in accordance with the said provisions;
(c) "original political party", in relation to a member of a House,
means the political party to which he belongs for the purposes of sub-
paragraph (1) of paragraph 2;
(d) "paragraph" means a paragraph of this Schedule.
2. Disqualification on ground of defection.—(1) Subject to the
provisions of 3[paragraphs 4 and 5], a member of a House belonging to any
political party shall be disqualified for being a member of the House—
(a) if he has voluntarily given up his membership of such political
party; or
(b) if he votes or abstains from voting in such House contrary to
any direction issued by the political party to which he belongs or by any
person or authority authorised by it in this behalf, without obtaining, in
either case, the prior permission of such political party, person or authority
and such voting or abstention has not been condoned by such political
party, person or authority within fifteen days from the date of such voting
or abstention.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-paragraph,—
(a) an elected member of a House shall be deemed to belong to the
political party, if any, by which he was set up as a candidate for election
as such member;
(b) a nominated member of a House shall,—
1. Tenth Schedule added by the Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985, s. 6
(w.e.f. 1-3-1985).
2. Certain words omitted by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 5
(w.e.f. 1-1-2004).
3. Subs. by s. 5, ibid., for "paragraphs 3, 4 and 5" (w.e.f. 1-1-2004).
(i) where he is a member of any political party on the date of
his nomination as such member, be deemed to belong to such
political party;
(ii) in any other case, be deemed to belong to the political
party of which he becomes, or, as the case may be, first becomes,
a member before the expiry of six months from the date on which
he takes his seat after complying with the requirements of article 99
or, as the case may be, article 188.
(2) An elected member of a House who has been elected as such otherwise
than as a candidate set up by any political party shall be disqualified for being a
member of the House if he joins any political party after such election.
(3) A nominated member of a House shall be disqualified for being a
member of the House if he joins any political party after the expiry of six months
from the date on which he takes his seat after complying with the requirements
of article 99 or, as the case may be, article 188.
(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing provisions of
this paragraph, a person who, on the commencement of the Constitution (Fifty-
second Amendment) Act, 1985, is a member of a House (whether elected or
nominated as such) shall,—
(i) where he was a member of political party immediately before
such commencement, be deemed, for the purposes of sub-paragraph (1) of
this paragraph, to have been elected as a member of such House as a
candidate set up by such political party;
(ii) in any other case, be deemed to be an elected member of the
House who has been elected as such otherwise than as a candidate set up
by any political party for the purposes of sub-paragraph (2) of this
paragraph or, as the case may be, be deemed to be a nominated member
of the House for the purposes of sub-paragraph (3) of this paragraph.

nodes.full_text:
1THE CONSTITUTION (APPLICATION TO JAMMU AND KASHMIR)
ORDER, 2019
C.O. 272
In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (1) of article 370 of the
Constitution, the President, with the concurrence of the Government of State of
Jammu and Kashmir, is pleased to make the following Order:—
1. (1) This Order may be called the Constitution (Application to Jammu
and Kashmir) Order, 2019.
(2) It shall come into force at once, and shall thereupon supersede the
Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954 as amended from
time to time.
2. All the provisions of the Constitution, as amended from time to time,
shall apply in relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir and the exceptions and
modifications subject to which they shall so apply shall be as follows:–
To article 367, there shall be added the following clause, namely:—
“(4) For the purposes of this Constitution as it applies in relation to
the State of Jammu and Kashmir–
(a) references to this Constitution or to the
provisions thereof shall be construed as references to the
Constitution or the provisions thereof as applied in relation
to the said State;
(b) references to the person for the time being
recognized by the President on the recommendation of the
Legislative Assembly of the State as the Sadar-i-Riyasat of
Jammu and Kashmir, acting on the advice of the Council of
Ministers of the State for the time being in office, shall be
construed as references to the Governor of Jammu and
Kashmir;
(c) references to the Government of the said State
shall be construed as including references to the Governor of
Jammu and Kashmir acting on the advice of his Council of
Ministers; and
(d) in proviso to clause (3) of article 370 of this
Constitution, the expression “Constituent Assembly of the
State referred to in clause (2)” shall read “Legislative
Assembly of the State”.”
1.Published with the Ministry of Law and Justice, (Legislative Department) notification
No. G.S.R. 551 (E), dated the 5th August, 2019, Gazette of India, Extraordinary,
Part II, Section 3, Sub-section (i).

APPENDIX III
1DECLRATION UNDER ARTICLE 370(3) OF THE CONSTITUTION
C.O. 273
In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (3) of article 370 read with
clause (1) of article 370 of the Constitution of India, the President, on the
recommendation of Parliament, is pleased to declare that, as from the 6th August,
2019, all clauses of the said article 370 shall cease to be operative except the
following which shall read as under, namely:—
“370. All provisions of this Constitution, as amended from time to
time, without any modifications or exceptions, shall apply to the State of
Jammu and Kashmir notwithstanding anything contrary contained in
article 152 or article 308 or any other article of this Constitution or any
other provision of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir or any law,
document, judgement, ordinance, order, by-law, rule, regulation,
notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of
India, or any other instrument, treaty or agreement as envisaged under
article 363 or otherwise.”.
1.Published with the Ministry of Law and Justice, (Legislative Department) notification
No. G.S.R. 562(E), dated the 6th August, 2019, Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II,
Section 3, Sub-section (i).

nodes.checks_and_balances: Laws passed by Parliament are subject to judicial review by the Supreme Court and High Courts under Articles 13, 32, and 226, and cannot violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).

explanations.advanced: Unlike the British Parliament, the Indian Parliament is not sovereign; it operates within a written federal Constitution with judicial review (Article 13) and Basic Structure limitations on Article 368.
explanations.beginner: Parliament is India's national law-making body. It has three parts: the President, the Lok Sabha (directly elected by citizens), and the Rajya Sabha (representing the States).
explanations.intermediate: Established under Article 79, Parliament exercises legislative power over the Union and Concurrent Lists, approves the Union Budget, and holds the Prime Minister and Cabinet accountable.
explanations.research: Parliament's bicameral design balances Westminster responsible government (Article 75(3) collective responsibility solely to Lok Sabha) with federal representation (Rajya Sabha's special powers under Articles 249 and 312).

nodes.full_text: The supreme legislative institution of the Republic of India, consisting of the President and two Houses: the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
powers_and_functions: Enacting laws on Union List (97/100 items) and Concurrent List (47/52 items) under Article 246
Constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368
Financial control over the Consolidated Fund of India (Articles 110, 112–117, 266)
Holding the Union Executive (Council of Ministers) accountable via questions, motions, and committees (Article 75(3))
Impeachment of the President (Article 61) and removal of Supreme Court/High Court Judges (Article 124(4))

nodes.checks_and_balances: Subject to dissolution by the President (Article 85(2)(b)), constitutional limits on legislative competence (Article 246), and Fundamental Rights scrutiny (Article 13).

explanations.advanced: The Lok Sabha embodies popular sovereignty in India's parliamentary system. Under Article 109, its dominance in financial legislation prevents upper-house deadlocks over supply, while Article 75(3) makes executive survival contingent on its confidence.
explanations.beginner: The Lok Sabha is the 'House of the People' where citizens directly elect Members of Parliament (MPs) every 5 years. Whichever party or coalition wins a majority here forms the central government.
explanations.intermediate: Composed under Article 81 with a 5-year term (Article 83(2)), the Lok Sabha controls the national purse (Money Bills under Article 110) and commands the survival of the executive under Article 75(3).
explanations.research: Constitutional debates (CAD Vol. VII & VIII) show the framers chose direct territorial election for the House of the People alongside Article 75(3) collective responsibility to anchor daily democratic accountability while subjecting delimitation to Articles 81–82.

nodes.full_text: The directly elected lower house of Parliament (up to 550 members elected from territorial constituencies by universal adult suffrage under Article 326). The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible solely to the Lok Sabha.
powers_and_functions: Exclusive power to introduce and pass Money Bills (Articles 109 & 110); Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days
Holds the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible under Article 75(3); can remove the government via a No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198)
Passes Demand for Grants and the Appropriation Bill authorizing expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India (Articles 113–114)
Co-equal legislative and constituent powers with Rajya Sabha on Ordinary Bills (Article 107) and Constitutional Amendment Bills (Article 368)

powers_and_functions: Writ Jurisdiction under Article 32 (itself a Fundamental Right) to enforce Part III rights via Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari
Exclusive Original Federal Jurisdiction under Article 131 for disputes between the Union and States or between States
Appellate Jurisdiction in constitutional, civil, and criminal matters (Articles 132–134) and Special Leave to Appeal (Article 136)
Power to do 'complete justice' in any cause or matter under Article 142; law declared by SC is binding on all courts in India (Article 141)
Advisory Jurisdiction on questions of law/fact referred by the President (Article 143) and Judicial Review of legislative/executive actions (Articles 13, 32)
nodes.summary: The apex constitutional court, final interpreter and guardian of the Constitution, and guarantor of Fundamental Rights (Article 32). Comprises the Chief Justice of India and up to 33 other Judges appointed under Article 124(2) via the Collegium system.

explanations.advanced: Through Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Puttaswamy (2017), the Supreme Court transformed liberty from compartmentalized textual freedoms (A.K. Gopalan, 1950) into an integrated 'Golden Triangle' (Articles 14, 19, 21) where any curtailment must satisfy legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality.
explanations.beginner: Liberty means the freedom to think, speak, move freely, practice your faith, and live your life with dignity without unfair government interference.
explanations.intermediate: Proclaimed in the Preamble ('LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship') and made enforceable in Articles 19–22 and 25–28, Indian constitutional liberty balances individual freedom with reasonable social restrictions.
explanations.research: Indian constitutionalism synthesizes liberal negative liberty (restraints on State power under Article 13) with republican and transformative positive liberty (enabling autonomy against both State and structural social domination).

nodes.full_text: Both negative liberty (freedom from arbitrary state restraint under Articles 19–22) and positive liberty (the conditions enabling self-realization and human dignity under Article 21 and Part IV). Dr. B.R. Ambedkar emphasized in his closing speech (25 Nov 1949) that liberty cannot be divorced from equality and fraternity.

explanations.advanced: In E.P. Royappa (1974), Indra Sawhney (1992), and Navtej Singh Johar (2018), the Supreme Court established that equality is dynamic and antithetical to arbitrariness, and that affirmative action under Article 16(4) is not an exception to equality but an emphatic facet of substantive equality.
explanations.beginner: Equality means every person is treated equally by the law and has an equal chance to succeed, regardless of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
explanations.intermediate: Articles 14–18 guarantee formal equality before the law while explicitly empowering the State to make special provisions (reservations and welfare measures) for historically disadvantaged groups.
explanations.research: The Indian equality code rejects purely color-blind/caste-blind formal symmetry in favor of asymmetric, anti-subordination substantive equality aimed at dismantling graded social hierarchy.

nodes.full_text: Combines formal equality ('equality before the law' and 'equal protection of the laws' under Article 14) with substantive and compensatory equality (prohibition of discrimination and affirmative action under Articles 15(4)–(6) and 16(4)–(6), and abolition of untouchability under Article 17).

explanations.advanced: [Philosophical — Fundamental Right & Value] Unanimously affirmed by a 9-Judge Constitution Bench in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and across the freedoms guaranteed by Part III. Encompasses bodily integrity, spatial privacy, informational self-determination, and decisional autonomy. Any state infringement (such as surveillance or data collection) must pass the four-prong Proportionality Test: (1) legality (existence of a law), (2) legitimate state aim (e.g., national security), (3) rational nexus & necessity (least restrictive measure), and (4) procedural guarantees against abuse. Constitutional Anchor: Articles 14, 19, 21 (Part III).

explanations.advanced: [Philosophical — Preamble Ideal & Basic Structure] Unlike strict Western church-state separation, Indian constitutional secularism combines equal freedom of conscience and religion for all (Article 25) and non-establishment (no state religion or religious tax under Article 27) with 'principled distance' that allows the State to reform social evils within religion (Article 25(2)(b)). Declared part of the Basic Structure in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994). Constitutional Anchor: Preamble, Articles 14, 15, 16, 25–30, 51A(e).

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Constitutional Doctrine] Propounded by a 13-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court (7:6 majority) in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): while Parliament has wide power under Article 368 to amend any part of the Constitution (including Fundamental Rights), the word 'amend' does not include the power to destroy, abrogate, or alter the 'basic structure or framework' of the Constitution (such as supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, secularism, rule of law, federalism, judicial review, separation of powers, and harmony between Parts III and IV). Constitutional Anchor: Article 368 interpreted in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) & Minerva Mills (1980).

Union of India (1978) and immortalized in Minerva Mills (1980) ('Three articles of our Constitution, and only three, stand between the heaven of freedom into which Tagore wanted his country to awake and the abyss of unrestrained power'). Holds that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive islands (overruling A.K. Gopalan, 1950), and any law depriving personal liberty under Article 21 must also pass the tests of non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and reasonableness under Article 19. explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Constitutional Doctrine] Held in Kerala Education Bill (1957), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), and Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are not antagonists but the 'conscience of the Constitution'—like two wheels of a chariot. Neither can destroy the other; courts must interpret them harmoniously so social-welfare goals are achieved through constitutional means. Constitutional Anchor: Parts III & IV (Articles 14, 19, 21, 31C, 37, 38, 39).

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Legal Test] Four-part constitutional standard for testing limitations on Fundamental Rights: (1) the measure must be designated for a proper/legitimate purpose, (2) the measures undertaken must be rationally connected to fulfilling that purpose, (3) there must be no alternative less invasive measure (necessity), and (4) there must be a proper balance between the importance of achieving the aim and the social importance of preventing the limitation on the constitutional right. Constitutional Anchor: Articles 14, 19, 21 (Modern Dental College 2016; Puttaswamy 2017).

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Federalism Doctrine] Judicial principles governing federal legislative competence: (1) Pith and Substance (State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, 1951): if the true nature and character of a law falls within a legislature's allotted list, incidental encroachment on another list does not invalidate it; (2) Colourable Legislation (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, 1953): 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly'; (3) Repugnancy (Article 254): on Concurrent List subjects, Union law prevails over conflicting State law unless the State law received Presidential assent under Article 254(2). Constitutional Anchor: Articles 245, 246, 254 & Seventh Schedule.

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Landmark Judgment (13-Judge Bench)] Heard by the largest bench in Supreme Court history (13 Judges) for 68 days. Background: Challenge to Kerala Land Reforms Acts and the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments. Core Constitutional Question: Is Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 unlimited? Holding (7:6 majority): Overruled Golaknath (1967) to hold that Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution including Fundamental Rights, BUT established the Basic Structure Doctrine—Parliament cannot use Article 368 to alter or destroy the basic structure or essential features of the Constitution. Also declared the Preamble an integral part of the Constitution. Constitutional Anchor: Article 368, Preamble, Part III (Articles 14, 19, 25, 26, 31C).

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Landmark Judgment (7-Judge Bench)] Background: Impounding of petitioner's passport under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 without giving a pre-decisional hearing or reasons. Core Constitutional Question: Does 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 mean any arbitrary statutory procedure (as held in A.K. Gopalan, 1950)? Holding: Overruled Gopalan's silo theory; established the Golden Triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21. Held that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be 'right and just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive', Infusing substantive due process and natural justice into Article 21. Constitutional Anchor: Articles 14, 19, and 21.

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Landmark Judgment (5-Judge Bench)] Background: Challenge to Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, which gave blanket primacy to all Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19 and declared that no constitutional amendment could be questioned in any court. Holding: Struck down both provisions as unconstitutional violations of the Basic Structure. Held that limited amending power and judicial review are themselves essential features of the Basic Structure, and that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is a bedrock feature of the Constitution. Constitutional Anchor: Articles 14, 19, 21, 31C, 368(4)–(5).

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Landmark Judgment (9-Judge Bench)] Background: Reference arising out of challenges to the biometric Aadhaar scheme when the Union argued (citing M.P. Sharma 1954 and Kharak Singh 1962) that the Constitution does not guarantee a fundamental right to privacy. Holding (Unanimous 9:0): Overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh; declared that the Right to Privacy is an inalienable natural right and an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III, grounded in human dignity and individual autonomy. Established the Proportionality Test for evaluating state surveillance, biometric systems, and data protection. Constitutional Anchor: Preamble, Articles 14, 19, 21 (Part III).

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Landmark Judgment (9-Judge Bench)] Background: Arbitrary dismissal of elected State Governments using President's Rule under Article 356. Holding: Federalism and Secularism are integral parts of the Basic Structure. The President's proclamation under Article 356 is not immune from judicial review; courts can examine whether the proclamation was based on relevant material or mala fide. Whether a Chief Minister enjoys a majority must be tested исключительно on the floor of the Vidhan Sabha (Floor Test), not in the Governor's subjective chamber. Constitutional Anchor: Article 356, Federalism, Secularism.

explanations.advanced: [Judicial — Historical Landmark Judgment (6-Judge Bench)] The Supreme Court's first major constitutional decision on preventive detention. The majority adopted a positivist, compartmentalized reading of Fundamental Rights (holding that Article 21 only required a procedure enacted by a valid statute, not natural justice or Article 19 reasonableness), while Justice Fazl Ali's famous dissent foreshadowed the integrated Golden Triangle adopted 28 years later in Maneka Gandhi (1978). Constitutional Anchor: Articles 19, 21, 22.

explanations.advanced: [Process — Financial Legislative Process] Defined strictly in Article 110(1) (taxation, Consolidated Fund borrowing/appropriation) and certified by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Article 110(3). Can be introduced ONLY in the Lok Sabha and ONLY on the recommendation of the President (Article 109(1), 117(1)). Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject a Money Bill; it must return it within 14 days with or without recommendations, which Lok Sabha may accept or reject (Article 109(2)). No Joint Sitting is permissible. Constitutional Anchor: Articles 109, 110, 111, 112–117.

explanations.advanced: [Process — Constituent Process] Initiated by introducing a Bill in either House of Parliament (never in a State Legislature; does not require prior Presidential recommendation). Must be passed in EACH House separately (no Joint Sitting allowed) by a Special Majority: a majority of the total membership of that House AND a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting. If the amendment seeks to change federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) (e.g., Presidential election Art. 54–55, Union/State executive & judiciary, Seventh Schedule, representation of States, or Art. 368 itself), it must ALSO be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before being presented to the President, who MUST give assent (`shall give his assent`, per 24th Amendment). Subject to Basic Structure review. Constitutional Anchor: Part XX (Article 368).

explanations.advanced: [Process — Democratic Process] Citizens aged 18+ vote under Universal Adult Suffrage (Article 326) in elections conducted by the Election Commission of India (Article 324) -> 543 MPs elected to Lok Sabha (Article 81) -> President appoints the leader commanding majority support (272+ seats) as Prime Minister (Article 75(1)) -> PM advises appointment of Council of Ministers -> Government proves majority via Vote of Confidence / Floor Test -> Council of Ministers remains in office so long as it retains the confidence of the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3); removable by No-Confidence Motion). explanations.advanced: [Process — Constitutional Remedy] Constitutional mechanism by which the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive/administrative orders against: (1) Fundamental Rights under Article 13(2), (2) Federal legislative competence under Articles 245–246, and (3) the Basic Structure Doctrine (for Constitutional Amendments). Enforced via the five prerogative writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari. Constitutional Anchor: Articles 13, 32, 131–136, 141–142, 226, 227, 245–246.

Enforced via the five prerogative writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari.

explanations.advanced: [Process — Emergency Provisions] Three constitutional emergency regimes converting the federal system into a unitary structure during crises: (1) National Emergency (Article 352) on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion (requires written Union Cabinet decision and special majority approval by both Houses within 1 month; Articles 20 & 21 can never be suspended per Article 359); (2) Failure of Constitutional Machinery in States / President's Rule (Article 356, subject to judicial review and floor test under S.R. Bommai); and (3) Financial Emergency (Article 360, never invoked in India's history). Constitutional Anchor: Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360).

explanations.advanced: [Process — Statutory Electoral Framework] While Part XV (Articles 324–329) establishes the constitutional skeleton of elections, Parliament enacted the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (allocation of seats, delimitation, voter registration, and electoral rolls) and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (qualifications and statutory disqualifications of MPs/MLAs, registration of political parties under Section 29A, conduct of elections, corrupt practices, and election petitions before High Courts). Constitutional Anchor: Articles 84, 102, 173, 191, 326, 327.
